```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
# First time only, run this once in the R console:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown"))
library(tidyverse)

min_group <- 10   # a group smaller than this is called "Other" (a Proposed threshold)
```

# 1. What this report does

This is a public list of Starbucks stores, downloaded from Kaggle. It is a learning project.
The snapshot date and how the data was collected are unknown.

The report does four things: loads the file, cleans it, and saves a clean file for Tableau.

# 2. Load the data

We read every column as text, so nothing is changed by accident. `na = character()` stops R
from treating the text "NA" as missing, because "NA" is also the country code for Namibia.
`read_csv` removes spaces at the start and end of each value.

```{r load}
raw <- read_csv("../data/raw/directory.csv",
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
                na = character())

# The original column names have spaces and a slash, so give them simple names
raw <- raw %>%
  rename(brand = Brand, store_number = `Store Number`, store_name = `Store Name`,
         ownership_type = `Ownership Type`, street_address = `Street Address`,
         city = City, state_province = `State/Province`, country = Country,
         postcode = Postcode, phone_number = `Phone Number`, timezone = Timezone,
         longitude = Longitude, latitude = Latitude)

dim(raw)    # expect 25600 rows and 13 columns
head(raw)
```


# 3. Clean the data

Each step below is small. Nothing is deleted except the one repeated Store Number.

```{r clean}
# Step 1: blank values become NA (R's way of saying "missing")
clean <- raw %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ na_if(.x, "")))

# Step 2: the text "NA" in postcode and city also means missing
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(postcode = na_if(postcode, "NA"),
         city = na_if(city, "NA"))

# Keep a copy of the cleaned data before removing the repeated Store Number
before_dedup <- clean

# Step 3: coordinates become numbers
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(longitude = as.numeric(longitude),
         latitude = as.numeric(latitude))

# Step 4: Check to confirm Grain using Store Number, to confirm one row = one store number.
# Keep one row per Store Number if likely. We put rows WITH coordinates first,
# so the row with coordinates is the one that stays.
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number(), .before = 1) %>%
  arrange(store_number, is.na(longitude)) %>%
  distinct(store_number, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  arrange(row_id)

nrow(raw) - nrow(clean)   # expect 1 row removed
```

# 4. Add a few simple columns

```{r features}
clean <- clean %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract the continent safely even if there is no space prefix
    tz_clean = if_else(str_detect(timezone, " "), str_split_i(timezone, " ", 2), timezone),
    continent = str_split_i(tz_clean, "/", 1)
  ) %>%
  select(-tz_clean)

clean
```

# 5. Explore the data

## Brand and ownership

```{r eda-brand}
clean %>% 
  count(brand, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    share_pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)
  )

clean %>% 
  count(
    ownership_type, sort = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    share_pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)
  )
```

## continent

```{r continent}
clean %>% 
  count(
    continent, sort = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    share_pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)
  )
```


## Countries

```{r}
# The 10 countries with the most stores
clean %>% 
  count(
    country, sort = TRUE
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    share_pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)
  ) %>%
  head(10)
```


# 6. Two quick checks (plots)

These are only to check the data. Make the final charts in Tableau.

```{r plot-country, fig.height=4}
clean %>%
  count(country, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Stores by country (top 10)", x = NULL, y = "Rows")
```

```{r plot-map, fig.height=4}
# If the data is right, this looks like a map of the world
ggplot(clean, aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.4) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Coordinate check")
```

# 8. Save the clean file for Tableau

```{r export}
dir.create("../data/processed", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(clean, "starbucks_clean.csv")
```

In Tableau, connect to `processed/starbucks_clean.csv` as a text file. Set `longitude` and
`latitude` to the Longitude and Latitude geographic roles. Keep `store_number`, `postcode`
and `phone_number` as text.

# Limits

- **Unknown:** the snapshot date, how the data was collected, and whether it covers every store.
- **Unknown:** what the Ownership Type and Brand labels mean in practice, and why a postcode
  or phone number is blank.
- The row removed in Step 4 is a repeated Store Number. That it is one store listed twice is my
  reading of your own check, not something the data proves.
- Coordinates were not checked against country borders.
